Parent: Okay. Look at this. Camilla Cream loved lima beans. But she never ate them. Do you know lima beans? It's like a little green bean like that. We don't eat it very much either. She never ate them. All her friends hated lima beans, and she wanted to fit in. Camilla was always worried about what other people thought of her.
Child: (nodding slightly, still looking at the tablet)

Parent: Today she was fretting even more than usual. Are you going to remember fretting? Do you know what that means? It means worrying. Are you worried? It was the first day of school, and she couldn't decide what to wear. There were so many people to impress. Do you know what that means? To impress? It means she wants people to like her. So, she's trying to do what she thinks other people want her to do.
Child: (smiling, still focused on the tablet)
Parent: She tried on 42 outfits. Do you even have 42 outfits? No, that's crazy. But none seemed quite right. She put on a pretty red dress and looked in the mirror. Then she screamed. Ahhh!
Child: (looking intrigued, leaning in closer to the tablet)
Parent: Her mother ran into the room, and she screamed, too.
Child: (looking at the tablet, seated close to the parent)

Parent: ""Oh my heavens! You're completely covered with stripes!" This was certainly true. Camilla was striped from head to toe. She looked like a rainbow. It looks like nice. Would you like to go to school like that? No?"
Child: (looking at the tablet, still paying attention)
Parent: "Mrs. Cream felt Camilla's forehead. "Do you feel all right?" she asked."
Child: (nodding slightly, still engaged and looking at the tablet)
Parent: ""I feel fine," Camilla answered, "but just look at me!""
Child: (leans in slightly, showing interest in the story)

Parent: ""You get back in bed this instant," her mother ordered. “You’re not going to school today.” Camilla was relieved. She didn’t want to miss the first day of school, but she was afraid of what the other kids would say. And she had no idea what to wear with those crazy stripes."
Child: (looking at the tablet, listening to the parent)

Parent: "That afternoon, Dr. Bumble came to examine Camilla. 'Most extraordinary!' he exclaimed. 'I’ve never seen anything like it. Are you having any coughing, sneezing, runny nose, aches, pains, chills, hot flashes, dizziness, drowsiness, shortness of breath, or uncontrollable twitching?'" (reading from the tablet)
Child: (still looking at the tablet, listening)
Parent: "'No,' Camilla told him. 'I feel fine.'" (continuing to read)
Child: (maintaining attention on the tablet)

Parent: "'Well then,' Dr. Bumble said, turning to Mrs. Cream, 'I don’t see any reason why she shouldn’t go to school tomorrow. Here’s some ointment that should help clear up those stripes in a few days. If it doesn’t, you know where to reach me.' And off he went." (reading further)
Child: (glancing at the parent)
Parent: "Oh look at that!" (pointing at the tablet)
Child: (looking at the book)
Parent: "The next day was a disaster. Everyone at school laughed at Camilla. They called her 'Camilla Crayon' and 'Night of the Living Lollipop.'"
Child: (still looking at the book)
Parent: "She tried her best to act as if everything were normal, but when the class said the Pledge of Allegiance, her stripes turned red, white, and blue, and she broke out in stars."
Child: (smiles, looking interested at the book)
Parent: "What is that? What do you think is happening there?"
Child: (continues looking at the book, looks engaged)
Parent: "The other kids thought this was great. One yelled, 'Let's see some purple polka dots!'"
Child: (slightly moving closer to the book, still engaged)
Parent: "Sure enough, Camilla turned all purple polka-dotty."
Child: (Looking at the tablet, sitting next to the parent)
Parent: Oops. Put it back...
Child: (Continues to look at the tablet, listening to the parent)

Parent: Someone else shouted, “Checkerboard!” and a pattern of squares covered her skin. Soon, everyone was calling out different shapes and colors, and poor Camilla was changing faster than you can change channels on a T.V. Aww, poor Camilla. Is it nice for him to do that?
Child: (No verbal response, but remains attentive)
Parent: No, not really.
Child: (Still looking at the tablet, listening carefully)
Parent: That night, Mr. Harms, the school principal, called.
Child: (Maintaining focus on the tablet, showing interest)

Parent: “I’m sorry, Mrs. Cream,” he said. “I’m going to have to ask you to keep Camilla home from school. She’s just too much of a distraction, and I’ve been getting calls from the other parents. They’re afraid those stripes may be contagious.”
Child: (looking at the parent)

Parent: "Do you know what contagious means? The parents are afraid the other kids could catch stripes. You know you catch a cough or a fever from other kids in your class? That's what it means, contagious. So the other kids could get the stripes."
Child: (listening attentively)
Child: (focused on the tablet)

Parent: "Camilla was so embarrassed. She couldn’t believe that two days ago everyone liked her. And now, nobody wanted to be in the same room with her. Her father tried to make her feel better. 'Is there anything I can get you, sweetheart?' he asked. 'No, thank you,' sighed Camilla. But what she really wanted was a nice plate of lima beans, but she had been laughed at enough for one day."
Child: (continues listening to the story)
Child: (still looking at the tablet)
Parent: "Hmm, well, yes, I see,” Dr. Bumble mumbled when Mr. Cream phoned the next day. 'I think I’d better bring in the specialists. We’ll be right over.'"
Child: (engaged with the story)
Child: (focused on the tablet)
Parent: "About an hour later, Dr. Bumble arrived with four people in long white coats. He introduced them to the Creams."
Child: (remains attentive to the story)
Child: (sitting next to the parent, looking at the tablet)
Parent: "This is Dr. Grop, Dr. Sponge, Dr. Cricket, and Dr. Young.”
Child: (continues looking at the tablet)
Child: (still watching the tablet, with hands placed on lap)
Parent: "Then the specialists went to work on Camilla. They squeezed and jabbed, tapped and tested. It was very uncomfortable. 'Well. It’s not the mumps,' concluded Dr. Grop."
Child: (remains focused on the tablet, slightly smiles)
Child: (keeps looking at the tablet screen)
Parent: "'Or the measles,' said Dr. Sponge."
Child: (maintains attention on the tablet)
Child: (looks at the tablet attentively)
Parent: "She has like a leopard leg."
Child: (nods slightly, continues to focus on the tablet)
Child: (looking at the tablet)
Parent: “Definitely not chicken pox,” put in Dr. Cricket.
Child: (continues looking at the tablet)
Parent: “Or sunburn,” said Dr. Young.
Child: (continues looking at the tablet)
Parent: “Try these,” said the specialists.
Child: (continues looking at the tablet)
Parent: They each handed her a bottle filled with different colored pills.
Child: (looking at the tablet with interest)
Parent: “Take one of each before bed,” said Dr. Grop.
Child: (watching the screen intently)
Parent: Then they filed out the front door, followed by Dr. Bumble.
Child: (continues looking at the screen)
Parent: Look at that!
Child: (slightly leans closer, focusing on the tablet)

Parent: That night, Camilla took her medicine. It was awful. When she woke up the next morning, she did feel different, but when she got dressed, her clothes didn’t fit. She looked in the mirror, and there, staring back at her, was a giant, multi-colored pill with her face on it.
Child: (looking at the tablet along with the parent)
Parent: Look at that.
Child: (continues looking at the tablet)
Child: (smiles)

Parent: Dr. Bumble rushed over as soon as Mrs. Cream called. But this time, instead of the specialists, he brought the experts. Dr. Gourd and Mr. Mellon were the finest scientific minds in the land. Once again, Camilla was poked and prodded, looked at and listened to. The experts wrote down lots of numbers. Then they huddled together and whispered. Dr. Gourd finally spoke.
Child: (assumes a curious expression, continues looking at the tablet)
Parent: “It might be a virus,” he announced with authority. Suddenly, fuzzy little virus balls appeared all over Camilla.
Child: Uh-oh! (continues looking at the tablet)
Child: (sitting next to parent, looking at the tablet)

Parent: “Or possibly some form of bacteria,” said Mr. Mellon. Out popped squiggly little bacteria tails. This must be the bacteria tails. Where's the virus? Do you want to see the virus? Where do you think is the virus, Toto?"
Child: (points at the tablet)
Parent: (smiles and continues reading)
Child: (looking at the tablet)
Parent: The green things.
Child: (points at the tablet)
Parent: There's the green thing, might be the bacteria tail or the fuzzy are the balls. The little balls...
Child: (continues looking at the tablet, hand close to the mouth)
Parent: (continues reading)
Child: (still looking at the tablet)
Parent: “Or it could be a fungus,” added Dr. Gourd. Instantly, Camilla was covered with different colored fungus blotches. The experts looked at Camilla, and then at each other.
Child: (seems engaged, continues looking at the tablet)
Parent: (points to the tablet, reading along)
Child: (sitting next to the parent, looking at the tablet)
Parent: "We need to go over these numbers again back at the lab," Dr. Gourd explained. "We’ll call you when we know something." (pointing at the tablet)
Child: (looking at the parent, leaning slightly closer)
Parent: What do you think is happening, Toto? (looking at the child, still pointing at the tablet)
Child: (responding, looking back at the parent)
Parent: The stuff [inaudible 00:07:16] when she tried on that shirt. I think that caused it. (continuing to look at the child)
Child: (nodding slightly, thinking)
Parent: You think the shirt had some virus particle and made her sick? Could be. We'll see. (continues pointing at the tablet)
Child: (looking at the tablet)
Parent: "By now, the T.V. news had found out about Camilla. Reporters from every channel were outside her house, telling the story of “The Bizarre Case of the Incredible Changing Kid.”
Child: (continues looking at the tablet)
Child: (glancing at the parent's hand pointing to the tablet)

Parent: "Soon, a huge crowd was camped out on the front lawn. The Creams were swamped with all kinds of remedies from psychologists, allergists, herbalists, nutritionists, psychics, an old medicine man, a guru, and even a veterinarian. Each so-called cure only added to poor Camilla’s strange appearance until it was hard to even recognize her."
Child: (focusing on the screen)
Child: (still looking at the tablet)
Parent: "Where do you think Camilla is? What's that on her back?"
Child: "A tail."
Child: (looking at parent)
Parent: "How do you think she got a tail?"
Child: "She sprouted roots and berries and crystals and feathers and a furry, long tail. But nothing worked."
Parent: (nodding and smiling at the child)
Child: (smiling back)
Child: (looking at the tablet screen, focused)
Parent: (pointing at the screen) "I think the veterinarian gave her a tail."
Child: (continues to look at the screen)

Parent: (pointing at the screen) "One day, a woman who called herself an environmental therapist claimed she could cure Camilla. ‘Close your eyes,’ she said. ‘Breathe deeply, and become one with your room.’"
Child: (still looking at the screen, attentive)
Parent: (pointing at the screen, placing hand on chin) "‘I wish you hadn’t said that,’ Camilla groaned."
Child: (continues to look at the screen)
Parent: (pointing at the screen, hand on chin) "Slowly, she started to melt into the walls of her room. Her bed became her mouth, her nose was a dresser, and two paintings were her eyes."
Child: (looking at the tablet, engaged)
Parent: Look at that. Do you see her nose? Oh, where's her mouth? Look out for her mouth. That's so cool.
Child: (watching the tablet attentively)
Parent: The therapist screamed and ran from the house.
Child: (still focused on the tablet)
Parent: “What are we going to do?” cried Mrs. Cream. “It just keeps getting worse and worse!”
Child: (continues to look at the tablet)

Parent: She began to sob. At that moment, Mr. Cream heard a quiet little knock at the front door. He opened it, and there was an old woman who was just as plump and sweet as a strawberry. “Excuse me,” she said brightly. “But I think I can help.” She went into Camilla’s room and looked around.
Child: (looking at the tablet)

Parent: (pointing at the tablet) “My goodness,” she said with a shake of her head. “What we have here is a bad case of stripes. One of the worst I’ve ever seen!” She pulled a container of small green beans from her bag. “Here,” she said. “These might do the trick.”
Child: (continues looking at the tablet)
Parent: (still pointing at the tablet) And she's feeding her the beans.
Child: (continues looking at the tablet)
Parent: (pointing at the tablet) “Are those magic beans?” asked Mrs. Cream.
Child: (continues looking at the tablet)
Parent: (pointing at the tablet) “Oh my, no,” replied the kind old woman. “There’s no such thing. These are just plain old lima beans. I’ll bet you’d like some, wouldn’t you?” she asked Camilla.
Child: (sitting next to the parent, looking at the tablet)

Parent: (pointing at the tablet screen) "Camilla wanted a big, heaping plateful of lima beans more than just about anything, but she was still afraid to admit it. 'Yuck!' she said. 'No one likes lima beans, especially me!'"
Child: (continuing to look at the tablet, engaged)

Parent: (pointing at the tablet screen) "'Oh, dear,' the old woman said sadly. 'I guess I was wrong about you.' She put the beans back in her bag and started toward the door. Camilla watched the old woman walk away. Those beans would taste so good. And being laughed at for eating them was nothing, compared to what she’d been going through. She finally couldn’t stand it."
Child: (attentively looking at the tablet)
Parent: (pointing at the tablet screen) "'Wait!' she cried. 'The truth is I really...'"
Child: (still focusing on the tablet)
Parent: (pointing at the tablet screen) "...love lima beans. I-"
Child: (looking at the tablet)
Parent: "...thought so," the...
Child: (still looking at the tablet, seems engaged)
Parent: ...the old woman said...
Child: (continues to look at the tablet, slightly leaning towards it)
Parent: ...with...
Child: (leans even closer to the tablet)
Parent: ...a smile. She took a handful of beans and put [crosstalk 00:10:29] them in Camilla’s mouth.
Child: (laughs and looks up at the parent briefly)
Child: (looking at the tablet)
Parent: “Mm,” said Camilla.
Child: (still looking at the tablet)
Parent: Mm...
Child: (remains focused on the tablet)
Parent: Suddenly the branches, feathers, and squiggly tails began to disappear. Then the whole room swirled around. When it stopped, there stood Camilla, and everything was back to normal.
Child: (continues to look at the tablet)
Parent: “I’m cured!” she shouted.
Child: (excitedly looks up at the parent)
Child: (focused on the tablet)
Parent: "It sounds different than most of the U's."
Child: (continues looking at the tablet)
Parent: "Yes," said the old woman.
Child: (remains engaged, looking at the screen)
Parent: "I knew the..."
Child: (nods slightly in anticipation)
Parent: "...real you was in there somewhere."
Child: (smiling, continues to watch the screen intently)

Parent: "She patted Camilla on the head. Then she went outside and vanished into the crowd. Afterward, Camilla wasn’t quite the same. Some of the kids at school said she was weird, but she didn’t care a bit. She ate all..."
Child: (leans closer to the tablet, appearing more interested)
Parent: "...the lima beans she wanted, and she never had even..."
Child: (still focused on the story, responding with a smile)
Child: (looking at the tablet, smiling)
Parent: "...even a touch-"
Child: (still looking at the tablet, smiling)
Parent: "...of stripes-"
Child: (still looking at the tablet, smiling)
Parent: "...stripes..."
Child: (pointing at the tablet, turns to the parent)
Parent: "...again."
Child: (looking at the tablet)
Parent: "Aww."
Child: "Look." (pointing at the tablet)
Parent: "What?"
Child: "A bow."
Parent: "Her bow's a little stripey? That's true, her bow is a little stripey. Anything else you want to talk about?"
Child: (smiling and nodding)
Parent: "I think she does look weird."
Child: "Don't! You don't tell kids at school that, do you?"
Parent: (looking interested)
Child: "I don't."
Parent: "No. Everybody can like how they look, Toto."
Child: (playfully touching the tablet)
Parent: "Back to the cover."
Child: (pointing at the tablet)
Parent: "Yeah, I think you want the first page? There?"
Child: (sitting next to the parent, looking at the tablet)
Parent: "She looks totally different."
Child: (looking at the tablet)
Parent: "Let's see. There she is, on that cover. Do you want to read another book? Do you want a short book or a long book?"
Child: "This book." (pointing at the tablet)
Parent: "Cloudy With a Chance of Meatballs? Another long book? Okay."
Child: (listening attentively, looking at the tablet)

Parent: "We were all sitting around the big kitchen table. It was Saturday morning. Pancake morning. Mom was squeezing oranges for juice. Henry and I were betting on how many pancakes we each could eat. And Grandpa was doing the flipping."
Child: (pointing at the tablet, with curiosity)
Parent: "What's on his head there?"
Child: (pointing at the tablet)

Parent: "Seconds later, something flew through the air headed toward the kitchen ceiling, and landed right on Henry. After we realized that the flying object was only a pancake, we all laughed, even Grandpa. Breakfast continued quite uneventfully. All the other pancakes landed in the pan. And all of them were eaten, even the one that landed on Henry."
Child: (sitting back, looking at the parent)
Parent: "That night, touched off by the pancake incident at breakfast, Grandpa told us the best tall-tale bedtime story he’d ever told."
Child: (leaning in, looking at the tablet)
Parent: "Across an ocean, over lots of huge bumpy mountains, across three hot deserts, and one smaller ocean... there lay the tiny town of Chewandswallow."
Child: (leaning forward, pointing)
Parent: "Please sit upright in your chair."
Child: (sitting upright, listening)

Parent: "In most ways, it was very much like any other tiny town. It had a Main Street lined with stores, and houses with trees and gardens around them, a schoolhouse, about three hundred people, and some assorted cats and dogs."
Child: (pointing at the tablet)
Parent: "You see that dog? I don't see any... oh, there's a dog. What is that guy doing?"
Child: "The cello."
Parent: "He's playing the cello?"
Child: (listening, looking at the tablet)
Parent: "But there were no food stores in the town of Chewandswallow. They didn’t need any. The sky supplied all the food they could possibly want."
Child: (pointing at the tablet, excitedly)
Parent: "There's a cat."
Child: (listening, looking at the tablet)

Parent: "The only thing that was really different about Chewandswallow was its weather. It came three times a day, at breakfast, lunch, and dinner. Everything that everyone ate came from the sky. Whatever the weather served, that's what they ate. But it never rained rain. It never snowed snow. And it never blew just wind. It rained things like soup and juice. It snowed mashed potatoes and green peas, and sometimes, the wind blew in storms of hamburgers."
Child: (looking closely at the tablet)
Parent: "What is that?"
Child: "Mashed potatoes."
Parent: "Oh, that's mashed potatoes? That looks like syrup. Is that orange juice?"
Child: "Yeah."
Parent: "The people could watch the weather report on television in the morning and they would even hear a prediction for the next day’s food."
Child: (pointing, looking curious)
Parent: "They got a bunch of juice, or soup? What do you think that is?"
Child: "Juice."
Parent: "Is that pie day? I think I would like pie day. What would you like it to be? Oh, chickens? I think she's getting chicken."
Child: (listening attentively, looking at the tablet)

Parent: "When the townspeople went outside, they carried their plates, cups, glasses, forks, spoons, knives, and napkins with them. That way they would always be prepared for any kind of weather. If there were leftovers, and there usually were, the people took them home and put them in their refrigerators in case they got hungry between meals."
Child: (looking at the tablet)
Parent: "What is that? Toast and sandwich day?"
Child: (sitting back, looking at the tablet)

Parent: "The menu varied. By the time they woke up in the morning, breakfast was coming down. After a brief shower of orange juice, low clouds of sunny-side up eggs moved in followed by pieces of toast. Butter and jelly sprinkled down for the toast. And most of the time it rained milk afterwards."
Child: "Mm, mm. I think even the squirrels like the toast with the jelly."

Parent: "For lunch one day, frankfurters, already in their rolls, blew in from the northwest at about five miles an hour. There were mustard clouds nearby. Then the wind shifted to the east and brought in baked beans. A drizzle of soda finished off the meal."
Child: (pointing at the tablet, with excitement)
Parent: "Look at that... hot dogs."
Child: (sitting back, looking at the tablet)

Parent: "Dinner one night consisted of lamb chops, becoming heavy at times, with occasional ketchup. Periods of peas and baked potatoes were followed by gradual clearing, with a wonderful jello setting in the west."
Child: (looking at the tablet, confused)
Parent: "Look at that. It's the jello. These are the-"
Child: "What does the jello setting mean?"
Parent: "Jello, you know what jello is. You ate that with Deborah this week. You remember? She maybe calls it gelatine. Gelatine? It's jello. Like that red stuff. [crosstalk 00:16:44]"
Child: "Setting?"
Parent: "Like a sun is setting in the West. Have you heard the sun is setting in the West?"
Child: "Uh-huh (affirmative)."
Parent: "That means like that. So it looks like the jello is going down."
Child: (sitting next to the parent, looking at the tablet)

Parent: "The Sanitation Department of Chewandswallow had a rather unusual job for a sanitation department. It had to remove the food that fell on the houses and sidewalks and lawns. The workers cleaned things up after every meal and fed all the dogs and cats. Then they emptied some of it into the surrounding oceans for the fish and turtles and whales to eat. The rest of the food was put back into the earth so that the soil would be richer for the people’s flower gardens."
Child: (still looking at the tablet)
Parent: "What is this? It looks like corn and pie."
Child: (nods slightly, maintaining attention on the tablet)
Parent: "Life for the townspeople was delicious until the weather took a turn for the worse."
Child: (glances at the parent's face momentarily, then back to the tablet)
Parent: "Do you know what this says? 'Spaghetti ties up town.'"
Child: (giggles softly)
Parent: "One day there was nothing but Gorgonzola cheese all day."
Child: (smiling, engaging with the text)
Parent: "That's kind of a stinky cheese. I don't know if you like that cheese. Did you ever eat blue cheese? Some people don't like it."
Child: (scratches head playfully)
Parent: "The next day there was only broccoli, all overcooked."
Child: (makes a face of mild disgust)
Parent: "Look at that soggy broccoli. Would you like to eat only broccoli all day long?"
Child: (shakes head in playful disapproval)
Parent: "And the next day there were brussels sprouts and peanut butter with mayonnaise."
Child: (in a voice showing curiosity)
Parent: "Would you like that? The kids don't look very happy. That's your birthday. You don't get birthday cake, you only get that."
Child: (shakes head emphatically, looking amused)
Parent: "Another day there was a pea soup fog. No one could see where they were going and they could barely find the rest of the meal that got stuck in the fog."
Child: (gasps slightly, clutching hands in excitement)
Parent: "Look at that huge pancake."
Child: (leans closer, intrigued)
Parent: "The food was getting larger and larger, and so were the portions. The people were getting frightened. Violent storms blew up frequently, and awful things were happening!"
Child: (visibly excited, pointing at the tablet)
Parent: "Look at that. I think that bird is happy. What is that? Is that donuts?"
Child: (squints at the screen, pondering)
Parent: "Bread."
Child: (nods in agreement)

Parent: "One Tuesday there was a hurricane of bread and rolls all day long and into the night. There were soft rolls and hard rolls, some with seeds and some without. There was white bread and rye and whole wheat toast. Most of it was larger than they had ever seen bread and rolls before. It was a terrible day. Everyone had to stay indoors. Roofs were damaged, and the Sanitation Department was beside itself. The mess took the workers four days to clean up, and the sea was full of floating rolls."
Child: (looks at the tablet intently)
Parent: "To help out, the people piled up as much bread as they could in their backyards. The birds picked at it a bit, but it just stayed there and got staler and staler."
Child: (rests head on hands, looking fascinated)

Parent: "There was a storm of pancakes one morning and a downpour of maple syrup that nearly flooded the town. A huge pancake covered the school. No one could get it off because of its weight, so they had to close the school."
Child: (nods enthusiastically, engaged)
Parent: "That is the biggest pancake I've ever seen."
Child: (in an agreeing tone)
Parent: "Mine, too."
Child: (leans in closer to the tablet)
Parent: "What?"
Child: (in an agreeing tone, more animated)
Parent: "Mine, too."
Child: (leans back slightly, looking at the parent)
Parent: "That's the biggest pancake you've ever seen?"
Child: (nods excitedly)
Parent: "Lunch one day brought 15-inch drifts of cream cheese and jelly sandwiches. People ate themselves sick and the day ended with a stomach ache."
Child: (laughs, covering mouth playfully)
Parent: "Whoa, so many sandwiches. What do you think this is?"
Child: (leans forward, looking curious)
Parent: "Ketchup twister!"
Child: (glancing at the parent, giggling)
Parent: "It's a ketchup twister?"
Child: (nods in amusement)

Parent: "There was an awful salt and pepper wind accompanied by an even worse tomato tornado. People were squeezing themselves silly and running to avoid the tomatoes. The town was a mess, and there were seeds and pulp everywhere. The Sanitation Department gave up. The job was too big."
Child: (leans forward, looking invested in the story)

Parent: "Everyone feared for their lives. They couldn’t go outside most of the time. Many houses had been badly damaged by giant meatballs. Stores were boarded up and there was no more school for the children."
Child: (rests head on hands, looking intrigued)
Parent: "You would like this day I think the best, right?"
Child: (engaged, looking at the tablet)
Parent: "Yeah."
Child: (still engaged, looking at the tablet)
Parent: "Yeah, donut day?"
Child: (watching the screen attentively)
Parent: "So a decision was made to abandon the town of Chewandswallow. It was a matter of survival."
Child: (smiling, hands on cheeks)
Parent: "Oh this guy got hit by a big hamburger. Those are big olives. You would like that too, right?"
Child: (smiling, engaged)
Parent: "And look! [crosstalk 00:20:43]"
Child: (pointing towards the tablet)
Parent: "Look at it! Which is your favorite?"
Child: (hands still on cheeks)
Parent: "Ice cream."
Child: (smiling, slightly turning towards the parent)

Parent: "Ice cream, I thought you would love this pickle too. And isn't this french fries? Look at those french fries. I think he's got a noodle on his head. What do you think that is? A noodle? [crosstalk 00:20:57]"
Child: (nodding)
Parent: "A noodle."
Child: (watching the tablet)
Parent: "The people glued together the giant pieces of stale bread sandwich-style with peanut butter, and took the absolute necessities with them, and set sail on their rafts for a new land."
Child: (still watching the tablet, hands on cheeks)
